body_text:
The Mean Value Theorem (Lagrange). Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$
be continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a, b]$ and
differentiable on the open interior $(a, b)$ with $a < b$. Then
there exists at least one point $c \in (a, b)$ such that:
$$ f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}. $$

*Proof*: Consider the secant difference function:
$$ g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}(x - a). $$ The
function $g$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on
$(a, b)$, and satisfies $g(a) = 0 = g(b)$. By the Extreme Value
Theorem, $g$ attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute
minimum on $[a, b]$.
- If $g$ is identically zero, then $g'(c) = 0$ for all
  $c \in (a, b)$.
- Otherwise, $g$ must attain a non-zero local extremum at some
  interior point $c \in (a, b)$. By Fermat's theorem on stationary
  points, the vanishing of the two-sided derivative at an interior
  extremum forces $g'(c) = 0$.

Computing $g'(c) = f'(c) - \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} = 0$ yields
the desired result.
